text: IT Operations comes to you with a familiar kind of request: build a New Laptop Request catalog item, track who asked for what and why, require a real written justification whenever someone picks a premium model, and file it somewhere sensible instead of a flat list with forty other things. This lab works through that exact request using everything this chapter covered.

First question: standard catalog item, or Record Producer? This request needs to be tracked, approved — someone has to sign off on hardware spend — and assigned to a fulfillment task so IT Operations can actually order and image the machine. That's the standard Request and Requested Item lifecycle doing real work, so this is built as a standard catalog item, not a Record Producer.

Next, placement and variables. The item is filed under an existing IT Equipment category rather than left uncategorized. Laptop Model becomes a Choice variable, so fulfillment never receives an unmappable answer. Business Justification becomes Multi Line Text. Both the requester's manager and cost center come from the organization's existing Requester Info Variable Set, attached rather than rebuilt from scratch.

IT Operations' real complaint — approvals getting rubber-stamped with no reason attached — is solved with a Catalog UI Policy. The condition checks whether Laptop Model is one of the designated premium options. The action makes Business Justification both visible and mandatory. For every other model, the field stays visible but optional, and fulfillment is never left guessing why a premium machine was approved.

Put together: a standard catalog item filed under IT Equipment, carrying a Choice variable and a Multi Line Text variable, a shared Variable Set for manager and cost center, and one Catalog UI Policy making justification mandatory exactly when it matters. Every piece traces back to a real decision this chapter taught, and none of it required a single line of server-side script.

That closes out Service Catalog Administration. Next up, Chapter Four begins with Notification Records and Triggers — how ServiceNow actually decides when and who to email about everything built in this chapter and the two before it.
